statements.quote: The best way to predict the future is to invent it.
A standard LLM can only use what it memorized during training.
Ask it about a document it never saw, and it either **hallucinates** or says *“I don't know.”*

Overlap ensures no information falls between the cracks.

- **HNSW** (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) \cite{malkov2018hnsw}: builds a multi-layer graph.
Searching “hops” through the graph, narrowing in on the target region, like navigating a city by jumping between landmarks.
*Most popular in production.*
- **IVF** (Inverted File Index): clusters vectors into Voronoi cells at index time.
At query time, only a few nearby cells are searched.
- **Product Quantization** \cite{jegou2011pq}: compresses vectors into compact codes, trading a tiny bit of accuracy for massive memory savings.
Result: with quantized indexes, a billion vectors can be queried in tens of milliseconds on a single machine — at the cost of some accuracy and a large memory footprint.
Type a query and see which “documents” match by cosine similarity.
This is a toy demo using tiny vectors, real systems use 768+ dimensions, but the principle is identical.
Each “document” and your query are mapped to a tiny vector using keyword heuristics (a stand-in for a real embedding model).
The system computes cosine similarity between your query vector and every document vector, then ranks them.
In production, the embedding model is a neural network and vectors have hundreds of dimensions.
RAG and ICL are **complementary**, not competing.
In fact, **RAG feeds into ICL**: the retrieved documents *become* the in-context examples the model reasons over.
The model reads examples/instructions in the prompt Limited to what fits in the context window The human (or a program) decides what to include Works for any task: translation, code, reasoning…

An automated retriever selects what to put in the prompt Can search over millions of documents , far beyond any context window Specialised for knowledge-grounded Q&A The LLM still uses ICL to reason over the retrieved chunks
ICL relies on whatever the user manually puts in the prompt.
RAG **automates the selection** using vector search.
The LLM itself doesn't know the difference, it just sees tokens in its context window either way.
The magic of RAG is in the retrieval step *before* the LLM runs.
Modern LLMs have ever-growing context windows: 128K tokens (GPT-4 Turbo), 200K (Claude 3), even 1M+ (Gemini 1.5).
Research shows that LLMs pay the most attention to the **beginning** and **end** of long contexts, often ignoring information buried in the middle \cite{liu2023lostmiddle}.
Even if a 200K-token window *can* hold your data, the model may fail to *use* it.

RAG mitigates this by shrinking the context to a handful of chunks, but it does not abolish the effect: a relevant chunk placed in the middle of even a short retrieved set can be underused, so ordering matters.
In practice, **RAG + long context** work together: RAG retrieves the top 10–20 chunks, and the long context window gives the model room to reason over all of them at once.
- **Garbage in, garbage out.** If the document store contains wrong information, RAG will confidently retrieve and present it.
- **Indirect prompt injection.** Because RAG feeds retrieved text straight into the prompt, malicious instructions hidden in a document can try to hijack the model (see the Security chapter).
- **Chunking matters.** If a critical fact is split across two chunks and neither is retrieved, the answer will be incomplete.
- **Embedding blind spots.** Embedding models can misjudge similarity, a query about “Python” (the snake) might retrieve docs about “Python” (the language).
- **Latency.** The retrieval step adds ~50–200 ms per query.
The happy path — embed the corpus, retrieve the nearest chunks, hand them to the model — is what the sections above walk (see also [Semantic search](vectorsearch.php)).

This deeper half is what happens in practice, and it is mostly about the parts the happy path hides — **how you cut the corpus into chunks** (the single highest-leverage, least-discussed knob), **how you combine keyword and semantic search**, **how you rerank** with a second, more expensive model, and — the half the demos never show — **why retrieval-augmented generation so often underperforms** and how to find out whether *your* failure is in the retrieval or the generation.
Before anything is embedded, the corpus must be **chunked** — cut into pieces, because the model will be asked to answer from a *few* of them, not the whole.

statements.quote: The trade is **recall versus context-dilution**, and it is the whole game.

statements.quote: A chunk that is *too small* splits a relevant answer across two chunks, so retrieving one gives you a partial, misleading piece (low recall of the *complete* answer).
statements.section: Chunking is a decision, not a default

statements.quote: A chunk that is *too big* pulls in a lot of irrelevant text along with the relevant bit, so the model's attention is *diluted* across a context full of noise (you retrieve the answer, but drowned in context).
statements.section: Chunking is a decision, not a default

statements.quote: There is no universal right size — it depends on the document and the question — which is why it is a *decision* you tune per corpus, not a number you copy from a template.

statements.quote: > The chunk is the atom of the system.
statements.section: Chunking is a decision, not a default

statements.quote: Get the atom wrong and no amount of better embedding, better fusion, or better model fixes it: you are asking the model to reconstruct a thought from the fragments of its neighbor.

statements.quote: But it is weak on **exact, rare terms**: a product ID, an error code, a proper noun, a specific API flag.

statements.quote: Those are the things a *lexical* retriever — **BM25** (\cite[Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009]{robertson2009bm25}) — is built for: it scores by term match, weighted by how rare the term is across the corpus, and it does not care whether the query and the document *mean* the same thing, only whether they *share* the right words.
statements.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

statements.quote: A query that is half paraphrase and half exact term ("how do I configure `max_tokens` for the gpt-4o model?") is answered best by *both* at once — the dense side finds "how do I configure", the lexical side finds "`max_tokens`" and "gpt-4o".
statements.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

statements.quote: **Hybrid search** retrieves with both and **fuses** the two ranked lists.
statements.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

statements.quote: The standard fusion is **reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)**: for each document, sum over the two lists a score that depends only on its *rank* in that list,

statements.quote: Cheap recall (BM25 + dense, fused by RRF) gathers a broad candidate set; an expensive cross-encoder then reads each (query, doc) pair and keeps only the best.
statements.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

statements.quote: You cannot run the cross-encoder first — it is too slow over the whole corpus.
statements.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

statements.quote: Dense and BM25 are **first-stage** retrievers: they are cheap, so they can score *all* of the corpus, but they do so *coarsely* — a dense model scores the query and a document *separately* (two encodings, one distance), so it never actually reads them together.

A **cross-encoder** is the **second-stage** reranker: it takes the query *and* a candidate document as a single input, runs them through a transformer *jointly*, and outputs a relevance score for that pair.
Because it reads the pair, it is far more precise — it can tell that a chunk *mentions* the topic but does not *answer* the question, which a first-stage similarity cannot.
A recurring failure is that a chunk, *out of context*, is not retrievable.
statements.section: Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time

statements.quote: A paragraph that says "the failure mode was severe" is a great answer — but if the word "failure" never appears in the query, no retriever finds it, because the chunk, standing alone, does not say what it is *about*.
statements.section: Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time

statements.quote: **Contextual retrieval** \cite[Ford, Anthropic (2024)]{contextualretrieval2024} addresses this at **index time**: before embedding a chunk, prepend a short piece of LLM-written context that orients the chunk ("this paragraph is from a post-mortem about the checkout service's 2024-03-14 incident, and it describes the failure mode"), so the *enriched* chunk is what gets embedded and retrieved.
statements.section: Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time

statements.quote: Reported to cut the retrieval-failure rate by roughly half \cite[Ford, Anthropic (2024)]{contextualretrieval2024}.
statements.section: Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time

statements.quote: The idea generalizes: retrieval quality is set at **index time** as much as query time, and you can spend LLM compute at index time — once, per chunk — to make each chunk self-sufficient.
statements.section: Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time

statements.quote: It is the retrieval analog of doing the hard work up front.
statements.section: Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time

statements.section: Why RAG underperforms: the honest half

statements.quote: The through-line: RAG is not a feature you add; it is a **pipeline with two failure points** (retrieval and integration), and each has its own diagnosis.
statements.section: Why RAG underperforms: the honest half

statements.quote: "Just add RAG" is not a free lunch because the two halves fail independently, and the second hides the first — a confidently wrong answer from a *good* model over a *bad* context is the hardest failure to see, because everything in the model looks fine.

statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: Its conceptual blueprint — a personal, queryable store of human knowledge with associative links between documents, retrieved at the moment of use to augment a human's thinking — was drawn in 1945 by \citeauthor{bush1945aswemaythink} (\citeyear{bush1945aswemaythink}) in *The Atlantic Monthly*, in an essay that became the founding text of hypertext and personal information retrieval.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: \citeauthor{bush1945aswemaythink} named the device the **memex** ("memory extender") and described it as a desk-sized electromechanical console that would store a personal library of microfilmed books and records, let the user consult them on translucent screens at will, and — this is the part the field remembered — allow the user to build **associative trails** between documents by stringing them together with named links, so that consulting one document would automatically pull up the next.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: The human mind operates by association.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: With one item in its grasp, it snaps instantly to the next that is suggested by the association of thoughts, in accordance with some intricate web of trails carried by the cells of the brain.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: [...] Selection by association, rather than indexing, may yet be mechanized.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: Bush's diagnosis of why such a device was needed has aged remarkably well.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: He calls the problem the *crisis of selection*: the volume of published knowledge had grown past any human's ability to keep up with, and the existing tools for finding it — Dewey indices, the Library of Congress catalog, professional abstracting services — were optimised for *retrieval by metadata* (title, author, subject) and were useless for the question the working scholar actually asks, which is *what do I already have in my head that connects to this*.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: Bush's answer was to mechanise a different operation: not "search by keyword", but **"follow a trail of associated items"**, where each item can name the next.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: The trail is the user's private graph of "this reminds me of that", which the memex stores and lets the user replay, share, and accumulate.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: Three differences matter.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: First, Bush's "association" was *human-defined* — the user built the trails — whereas modern dense retrieval learns associations from co-occurrence statistics; this is Bush in spirit (associative access) but not in mechanism (machine-learned similarity).
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: Second, Bush's device **augmented a human reader**, not an LLM; the LLM is the new reader, and the augmentation has been upgraded from "the user's cognition" to "the model's prompt".
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: Third, and most strikingly, Bush's essay did **not** anticipate the cheapness constraint that defines modern RAG: he imagined dedicated microfilm hardware in every office, while contemporary RAG assumes the documents already live somewhere (the web, a wiki, an email archive) and only the *index* and the *retriever* are new.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: In every other respect — personal library, associative access, named links, retrieved at the moment of use to support the user's train of thought — \citeauthor{bush1945aswemaythink}'s memex is the engineering plan a modern RAG system executes eighty years later.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: Two things did not have to wait eighty years.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: \citeauthor{bush1945aswemaythink}'s central *technical* prediction — that information would be retrieved by **associative** rather than by **alphabetical or categorical** links — is now the standard practice in retrieval: dense vectors retrieve by learned similarity, not by category.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: And his central *cultural* prediction — that the volume of human knowledge was about to outrun any individual's ability to navigate it without mechanical aid — is now the universal assumption of every knowledge-worker's morning.
statements.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

statements.quote: Long before neural embeddings, retrieval was lexical and statistical.
statements.section: Before embeddings: SMART, tf-idf, and BM25

statements.quote: Gerard Salton's SMART system represented documents as vectors of term weights and ranked them by cosine similarity, the direct ancestor of today's vector scoring.
statements.section: Before embeddings: SMART, tf-idf, and BM25

statements.quote: The weighting scheme now called tf-idf — term frequency down-weighted by how rare a term is across the collection — grew out of that work, and the probabilistic Okapi BM25 ranker, developed in the 1990s, is still a hard baseline \cite{salton1975vectorspace, salton1988termweighting, robertson2009bm25}.
statements.section: Before embeddings: SMART, tf-idf, and BM25

statements.quote: Modern hybrid RAG runs this old machinery beside its embeddings.
statements.section: Before embeddings: SMART, tf-idf, and BM25

statements.quote: Open-domain question answering turned retrieval into a benchmark problem.
The TREC QA tracks of the late 1990s asked systems to answer factoid questions from a large text collection, joining retrieval and answer extraction in one pipeline \cite{voorhees1999trecqa}.
SQuAD (2016) then isolated the reading-comprehension half: given a paragraph, find the answer span \cite{rajpurkar2016squad}.
The two-stage pattern — retrieve passages, then read them — is exactly the shape of RAG.
The neural turn came when retrieval itself was trained.

Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) replaced sparse term matching with two BERT encoders, one for questions and one for passages, trained so that a question's vector is close to its gold passage; it beat BM25 on open-domain QA \cite{karpukhin2020dpr}.
REALM went further, pre-training a language model with a learned retriever and treating the retrieved document as a latent variable \cite{guu2020realm}.
These papers made retrieval a differentiable, learned component rather than a fixed inverted index.
Lewis et al.'s RAG (2020) paired a DPR retriever with a seq2seq generator and marginalised over retrieved passages during generation \cite{lewis2020rag}.

RETRO retrieved from trillions of tokens at the level of token chunks and fused the retrieved neighbours into the transformer's attention \cite{borgeaud2022retro}; Atlas showed that a strong retriever plus a modest reader could reach few-shot state of the art on knowledge-intensive tasks \cite{izacard2022atlas}.

Self-RAG later trained a model to emit reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and whether a passage supports the claim \cite{asai2023selfrag}, while GraphRAG built an entity-and-relation graph over the corpus and summarised its communities to answer global questions \cite{edge2024graphrag}.

How is search so fast?

- **HNSW** (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) \cite{malkov2018hnsw}: builds a multi-layer graph. Searching “hops” through the graph, narrowing in on the target region, like navigating a city by jumping between landmarks. *Most popular in production.*
- **IVF** (Inverted File Index): clusters vectors into Voronoi cells at index time. At query time, only a few nearby cells are searched.
- **Product Quantization** \cite{jegou2011pq}: compresses vectors into compact codes, trading a tiny bit of accuracy for massive memory savings.
Result: with quantized indexes, a billion vectors can be queried in tens of milliseconds on a single machine — at the cost of some accuracy and a large memory footprint.
RAG in context
🔍 Interactive: Similarity Search Demo
Type a query and see which “documents” match by cosine similarity. This is a toy demo using tiny vectors, real systems use 768+ dimensions, but the principle is identical.
🔎 Search

How does this demo work? Each “document” and your query are mapped to a tiny vector using keyword heuristics (a stand-in for a real embedding model). The system computes cosine similarity between your query vector and every document vector, then ranks them. In production, the embedding model is a neural network and vectors have hundreds of dimensions.
RAG vs. In-Context Learning (ICL)
RAG and ICL are **complementary**, not competing. In fact, **RAG feeds into ICL**: the retrieved documents *become* the in-context examples the model reasons over.
In-Context Learning
The model reads examples/instructions in the prompt Limited to what fits in the context window The human (or a program) decides what to include Works for any task: translation, code, reasoning…
RAG

An automated retriever selects what to put in the prompt Can search over millions of documents , far beyond any context window Specialised for knowledge-grounded Q&A The LLM still uses ICL to reason over the retrieved chunks
Why do they *seem* different?

ICL relies on whatever the user manually puts in the prompt. RAG **automates the selection** using vector search. The LLM itself doesn't know the difference, it just sees tokens in its context window either way. The magic of RAG is in the retrieval step *before* the LLM runs.
RAG and Long Context Windows
Modern LLMs have ever-growing context windows: 128K tokens (GPT-4 Turbo), 200K (Claude 3), even 1M+ (Gemini 1.5). So why bother with RAG?
The “Lost in the Middle” Problem

Research shows that LLMs pay the most attention to the **beginning** and **end** of long contexts, often ignoring information buried in the middle \cite{liu2023lostmiddle}. Even if a 200K-token window *can* hold your data, the model may fail to *use* it.

RAG mitigates this by shrinking the context to a handful of chunks, but it does not abolish the effect: a relevant chunk placed in the middle of even a short retrieved set can be underused, so ordering matters.
In practice, **RAG + long context** work together: RAG retrieves the top 10–20 chunks, and the long context window gives the model room to reason over all of them at once.
Making RAG work
Limitations & Failure Modes
- **Garbage in, garbage out.** If the document store contains wrong information, RAG will confidently retrieve and present it.
- **Indirect prompt injection.** Because RAG feeds retrieved text straight into the prompt, malicious instructions hidden in a document can try to hijack the model (see the Security chapter).
- **Chunking matters.** If a critical fact is split across two chunks and neither is retrieved, the answer will be incomplete.
- **Embedding blind spots.** Embedding models can misjudge similarity, a query about “Python” (the snake) might retrieve docs about “Python” (the language).
- **Latency.** The retrieval step adds ~50–200 ms per query.
Retrieval, in Depth

The happy path — embed the corpus, retrieve the nearest chunks, hand them to the model — is what the sections above walk (see also [Semantic search](vectorsearch.php)). This deeper half is what happens in practice, and it is mostly about the parts the happy path hides — **how you cut the corpus into chunks** (the single highest-leverage, least-discussed knob), **how you combine keyword and semantic search**, **how you rerank** with a second, more expensive model, and — the half the demos never show — **why retrieval-augmented generation so often underperforms** and how to find out whether *your* failure is in the retrieval or the generation.
Chunking is a decision, not a default
blocks.section: Chunking is a decision, not a default

blocks.quote: Before anything is embedded, the corpus must be **chunked** — cut into pieces, because the model will be asked to answer from a *few* of them, not the whole. The chunk is the **unit of retrieval**: it is the granularity at which "relevant" is decided and at which context is *spent*. And its size and boundaries are the highest-leverage choice in the whole pipeline, because they set two opposing costs at once.
blocks.section: Chunking is a decision, not a default

blocks.quote: The standard cuts, and what each optimizes:
blocks.section: Chunking is a decision, not a default

blocks.quote: The trade is **recall versus context-dilution**, and it is the whole game. A chunk that is *too small* splits a relevant answer across two chunks, so retrieving one gives you a partial, misleading piece (low recall of the *complete* answer). A chunk that is *too big* pulls in a lot of irrelevant text along with the relevant bit, so the model's attention is *diluted* across a context full of noise (you retrieve the answer, but drowned in context). There is no universal right size — it depends on the document and the question — which is why it is a *decision* you tune per corpus, not a number you copy from a template.
blocks.section: Chunking is a decision, not a default

blocks.quote: > The chunk is the atom of the system. Get the atom wrong and no amount of better embedding, better fusion, or better model fixes it: you are asking the model to reconstruct a thought from the fragments of its neighbor.
blocks.section: Chunking is a decision, not a default

blocks.quote: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions
blocks.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

blocks.quote: [Dense](vectorsearch.php) retrieval asks "which chunks are *semantically close* to this query?" — great for **paraphrase** (the query "how do I undo my last commit" matches "reverting a commit" even though no word is shared). But it is weak on **exact, rare terms**: a product ID, an error code, a proper noun, a specific API flag. Those are the things a *lexical* retriever — **BM25** (\cite[Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009]{robertson2009bm25}) — is built for: it scores by term match, weighted by how rare the term is across the corpus, and it does not care whether the query and the document *mean* the same thing, only whether they *share* the right words.
blocks.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

blocks.quote: A query that is half paraphrase and half exact term ("how do I configure `max_tokens` for the gpt-4o model?") is answered best by *both* at once — the dense side finds "how do I configure", the lexical side finds "`max_tokens`" and "gpt-4o". **Hybrid search** retrieves with both and **fuses** the two ranked lists. The standard fusion is **reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)**: for each document, sum over the two lists a score that depends only on its *rank* in that list,
blocks.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

blocks.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

blocks.quote: The two-stage funnel. Cheap recall (BM25 + dense, fused by RRF) gathers a broad candidate set; an expensive cross-encoder then reads each (query, doc) pair and keeps only the best. You cannot run the cross-encoder first — it is too slow over the whole corpus.
blocks.section: Hybrid search: BM25 and dense are different questions

blocks.quote: Reranking: the expensive second look

Dense and BM25 are **first-stage** retrievers: they are cheap, so they can score *all* of the corpus, but they do so *coarsely* — a dense model scores the query and a document *separately* (two encodings, one distance), so it never actually reads them together. A **cross-encoder** is the **second-stage** reranker: it takes the query *and* a candidate document as a single input, runs them through a transformer *jointly*, and outputs a relevance score for that pair. Because it reads the pair, it is far more precise — it can tell that a chunk *mentions* the topic but does not *answer* the question, which a first-stage similarity cannot.
Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time
blocks.section: Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time

blocks.quote: A recurring failure is that a chunk, *out of context*, is not retrievable. A paragraph that says "the failure mode was severe" is a great answer — but if the word "failure" never appears in the query, no retriever finds it, because the chunk, standing alone, does not say what it is *about*. **Contextual retrieval** \cite[Ford, Anthropic (2024)]{contextualretrieval2024} addresses this at **index time**: before embedding a chunk, prepend a short piece of LLM-written context that orients the chunk ("this paragraph is from a post-mortem about the checkout service's 2024-03-14 incident, and it describes the failure mode"), so the *enriched* chunk is what gets embedded and retrieved. Reported to cut the retrieval-failure rate by roughly half \cite[Ford, Anthropic (2024)]{contextualretrieval2024}.
blocks.section: Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time

blocks.quote: The idea generalizes: retrieval quality is set at **index time** as much as query time, and you can spend LLM compute at index time — once, per chunk — to make each chunk self-sufficient. It is the retrieval analog of doing the hard work up front.
blocks.section: Contextual retrieval: fix the chunk at index time

blocks.quote: Why RAG underperforms: the honest half
blocks.section: Why RAG underperforms: the honest half

blocks.quote: None of the above is a substitute for the fact that RAG *fails*, and the failure modes are structural (\cite[Gao et al., 2023]{ragsurvey2023}):
blocks.section: Why RAG underperforms: the honest half

blocks.quote: The through-line: RAG is not a feature you add; it is a **pipeline with two failure points** (retrieval and integration), and each has its own diagnosis. "Just add RAG" is not a free lunch because the two halves fail independently, and the second hides the first — a confidently wrong answer from a *good* model over a *bad* context is the hardest failure to see, because everything in the model looks fine.

blocks.quote: Summary
| Question | Answer |
| What is RAG? | Fetch relevant docs $\rightarrow$ inject into prompt $\rightarrow$ LLM answers grounded in evidence |
| How is data stored? | As dense vectors in a vector DB, indexed with ANN algorithms like HNSW |
| RAG vs. ICL? | ICL = manual prompt engineering. RAG = automated retrieval that *feeds* ICL. Complementary |
| RAG vs. long context? | RAG searches millions of docs cheaply. Long context holds ~1 book expensively. Best used together |
| Are the LLM's weights changed? | **No.** RAG only changes the *input*. The model itself is untouched |
History
Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: The RAG pipeline described in this chapter has a longer ancestry than 2020. Its conceptual blueprint — a personal, queryable store of human knowledge with associative links between documents, retrieved at the moment of use to augment a human's thinking — was drawn in 1945 by \citeauthor{bush1945aswemaythink} (\citeyear{bush1945aswemaythink}) in *The Atlantic Monthly*, in an essay that became the founding text of hypertext and personal information retrieval. \citeauthor{bush1945aswemaythink} named the device the **memex** ("memory extender") and described it as a desk-sized electromechanical console that would store a personal library of microfilmed books and records, let the user consult them on translucent screens at will, and — this is the part the field remembered — allow the user to build **associative trails** between documents by stringing them together with named links, so that consulting one document would automatically pull up the next.
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: The human mind operates by association. With one item in its grasp, it snaps instantly to the next that is suggested by the association of thoughts, in accordance with some intricate web of trails carried by the cells of the brain. [...] Selection by association, rather than indexing, may yet be mechanized.
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: Bush's diagnosis of why such a device was needed has aged remarkably well. He calls the problem the *crisis of selection*: the volume of published knowledge had grown past any human's ability to keep up with, and the existing tools for finding it — Dewey indices, the Library of Congress catalog, professional abstracting services — were optimised for *retrieval by metadata* (title, author, subject) and were useless for the question the working scholar actually asks, which is *what do I already have in my head that connects to this*. Bush's answer was to mechanise a different operation: not "search by keyword", but **"follow a trail of associated items"**, where each item can name the next. The trail is the user's private graph of "this reminds me of that", which the memex stores and lets the user replay, share, and accumulate.
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: Read against the present chapter, the mapping to RAG is exact:
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: | Memex (1945) | Modern RAG |
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: | Personal library of microfilmed documents | A vector index of an organisation's documents |
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: | "Selection by association" | Embedding-based semantic search (or hybrid BM25 + dense) |
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: | Stored, named **trails** linking documents | Stored, retrieved **chunks** injected into an LLM prompt |
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: | "The human mind snaps instantly to the next item" | The LLM attends over retrieved context to produce the next token |
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: | Consulting a doc on the translucent screen | Reading a chunk out of a vector DB at query time |
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: | The memex user's associative memory | The LLM's context window |
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: Three differences matter. First, Bush's "association" was *human-defined* — the user built the trails — whereas modern dense retrieval learns associations from co-occurrence statistics; this is Bush in spirit (associative access) but not in mechanism (machine-learned similarity). Second, Bush's device **augmented a human reader**, not an LLM; the LLM is the new reader, and the augmentation has been upgraded from "the user's cognition" to "the model's prompt". Third, and most strikingly, Bush's essay did **not** anticipate the cheapness constraint that defines modern RAG: he imagined dedicated microfilm hardware in every office, while contemporary RAG assumes the documents already live somewhere (the web, a wiki, an email archive) and only the *index* and the *retriever* are new. In every other respect — personal library, associative access, named links, retrieved at the moment of use to support the user's train of thought — \citeauthor{bush1945aswemaythink}'s memex is the engineering plan a modern RAG system executes eighty years later.
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: Two things did not have to wait eighty years. \citeauthor{bush1945aswemaythink}'s central *technical* prediction — that information would be retrieved by **associative** rather than by **alphabetical or categorical** links — is now the standard practice in retrieval: dense vectors retrieve by learned similarity, not by category. And his central *cultural* prediction — that the volume of human knowledge was about to outrun any individual's ability to navigate it without mechanical aid — is now the universal assumption of every knowledge-worker's morning.
blocks.section: Bush 1945: The Memex, Hypertext, and Personal Information Retrieval

blocks.quote: Before embeddings: SMART, tf-idf, and BM25
blocks.section: Before embeddings: SMART, tf-idf, and BM25

blocks.quote: Long before neural embeddings, retrieval was lexical and statistical. Gerard Salton's SMART system represented documents as vectors of term weights and ranked them by cosine similarity, the direct ancestor of today's vector scoring. The weighting scheme now called tf-idf — term frequency down-weighted by how rare a term is across the collection — grew out of that work, and the probabilistic Okapi BM25 ranker, developed in the 1990s, is still a hard baseline \cite{salton1975vectorspace, salton1988termweighting, robertson2009bm25}. Modern hybrid RAG runs this old machinery beside its embeddings.
blocks.section: Before embeddings: SMART, tf-idf, and BM25

blocks.quote: Open-domain QA: retrieve, then read

Open-domain question answering turned retrieval into a benchmark problem. The TREC QA tracks of the late 1990s asked systems to answer factoid questions from a large text collection, joining retrieval and answer extraction in one pipeline \cite{voorhees1999trecqa}. SQuAD (2016) then isolated the reading-comprehension half: given a paragraph, find the answer span \cite{rajpurkar2016squad}. The two-stage pattern — retrieve passages, then read them — is exactly the shape of RAG.
Dense retrieval: DPR and REALM

The neural turn came when retrieval itself was trained. Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) replaced sparse term matching with two BERT encoders, one for questions and one for passages, trained so that a question's vector is close to its gold passage; it beat BM25 on open-domain QA \cite{karpukhin2020dpr}. REALM went further, pre-training a language model with a learned retriever and treating the retrieved document as a latent variable \cite{guu2020realm}. These papers made retrieval a differentiable, learned component rather than a fixed inverted index.
RAG, RETRO, Atlas, Self-RAG, GraphRAG

Lewis et al.'s RAG (2020) paired a DPR retriever with a seq2seq generator and marginalised over retrieved passages during generation \cite{lewis2020rag}. RETRO retrieved from trillions of tokens at the level of token chunks and fused the retrieved neighbours into the transformer's attention \cite{borgeaud2022retro}; Atlas showed that a strong retriever plus a modest reader could reach few-shot state of the art on knowledge-intensive tasks \cite{izacard2022atlas}. Self-RAG later trained a model to emit reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and whether a passage supports the claim \cite{asai2023selfrag}, while GraphRAG built an entity-and-relation graph over the corpus and summarised its communities to answer global questions \cite{edge2024graphrag}.
